headline: Place one queen per row
statement: Place n queens on an n by n chessboard so none share a row, column, or diagonal. Return every distinct board, with Q for a queen and . for an empty square, in any order.
intuition: Place one queen in each row. Before choosing a column, check whether another queen already uses that column or either diagonal. If no later row can be filled, remove the last queen and try a different column. This avoids exploring boards that already contain an attack.
approach: Recursively choose a column in the next row.
Reject columns or diagonals already occupied; record a safe queen.
Recurse into the next row, then undo all three occupancy records.
When n rows are filled, construct a board from the chosen columns.
correctness: One queen per recursive row enforces row uniqueness. The sets enforce column and diagonal uniqueness. Each legal board has one sequence of column choices explored by the search, and undoing each choice makes sibling branches independent; thus all and only valid boards are emitted once.
bruteForce: List every assignment of n columns to n rows and check conflicts: n^n candidates.

complexity.explanation: Let S be the number of solutions. Column uniqueness bounds valid prefixes by permutations; trying n columns at those prefixes gives a safe O(n*n!) search bound. Constructing S independent n-by-n boards costs O(S*n²). Together these are bounded by O(n!*n²). Working sets, placement and recursion need O(n), excluding O(S*n²) output.

pitfalls: The two diagonal keys are row-column and row+column.
Remove occupancy marks after returning from recursion.
n=2 and n=3 have no solutions.
